abstract: As AI chatbots enter traditionally human domains like moral guidance, questions arise about their intersection with traditional frameworks like religion. While many assume religious individuals will resist AI intrusion in the moral sphere, we found the opposite. Across two pre-registered studies (stratified U.S. sample, *N*=695), religious engagement and identity were consistently associated with greater openness to seeking moral advice from AI. To understand intervening psychological factors, we conducted first-pass parallel mediation analyses using cross-sectional data. These models indicate the relationship is statistically accounted for primarily by a disposition to seek multi-source moral guidance, and secondarily by perceived authority of AI. Making no causal claims, we invite future experimental work manipulating these mediators to establish causality. Rather than shielding individuals from AI's moral appeal, this study indicates religiosity may systematically facilitate it. These findings carry broad societal implications for AI-mediated moral guidance, requiring coordinated attention from technologists, faith communities, and policymakers.
